newsitem.title: CHINA: FOCUS-China shares have mixed reaction to gov't mo.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-China shares have mixed reaction to gov't mo.

text.p: Chinese stocks markets ended mixed on Friday as the market digested a move by Beijing to wrest back control over the country's two major exchanges.
B shares -- those allowed to foreign investors -- shrugged off the long-rumoured announcement, closing up 8.92 percent to 87.676 points in Shanghai and rising 4.96 percent or 158.73 in Shenzhen.
But A shares responded warily, since previous government crackdown measures had been aimed squarely at the A share market, brokers said.
Shanghai A shares fell 2.47 percent to 1,188.824 points, while Shenzhen A's lost 1.78 percent to 375.20.
Longer-term, the government's move should leave room for broad-based share price gains, analysts said.
The measure was the latest in a series of crackdowns since May aimed at curbing speculation and analysts expected it would be the last for the time being.

China's State Council, or cabinet, on Friday announced it was putting control over the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock markets back into the hands of the market watchdog, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC).
In a long-anticipated announcement, the State Council also said Tu Guangshao would replace Yang Xianghai as president of the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

"If you want to look for broader meaning then it's positive," said Bruce Richardson, chief representative for HG Asia in Shanghai. "They're sending in new management to make sure people behave themselves."
In the future, selection of the chairman, vice chairman, president and vice president of both the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock markets would be subject to CSRC approval.
The move was needed since China must improve its regulatory environment to persuade foreign fund managers to sink money into its stock markets, analysts said.

Although the action appeared drastic, the stock markets have never enjoyed complete independence since their founding seven years ago, and the latest move showed the importance the top leadership has placed on developing the capital markets, they said.

"The Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges have never had the power to list shares on their own," said John Crossman, chief representative for Jardine Fleming Securities. "They were always dependent on the regulatory authorities."

Shanghai Stock Exchange officials said Beijing had left them in the dark about exactly how it would flex its new muscles over the markets, but concrete details were likely to emerge in one or two weeks.
Exchange officials sought to reassure investors that the move would have little impact and was part of the growing pains of China's stock markets.
"It (the centralisation move) won't have any effect because the development of the market is like this," said one Shanghai exchange official.

Beijing in July formally announced it had removed the former head of the market watchdog CSRC as part of its shake-up of the securities industry, which has included fining banks and securities firms for speculation.
The stock markets registered spectacular gains between January and April of this year, before the government was forced to rein in the rises in May due to worries over financial risk.
